reason: The text explicitly frames the conflict in national and demographic terms: the Pharaoh expresses concern to his people (עַמּוֹ) about the Israelite population (עַם בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל) being numerous and mighty, and fears they will join with Egypt's enemies in war. The conflict is presented as a collective threat based on population size and military power, not as a personal grievance (the new Pharaoh 'did not know Joseph' personally) nor as a religious dispute. The ensuing oppression is depicted as state-level institutional coercion—taskmasters and forced labor—directed at the Israelite people as a national group.
story: The Pharaoh turns on the Hebrews
